title: Andy Taylor Was Full of Surprises: Six Deep-Dive Career Moments
summary: Following his death at the age of 65, Billboard has highlighted some impressive, but overlooked moments from Andy Taylor’s Hall of Fame career.
content: Andy Taylor , the founding guitarist with Duran Duran , who passed away Monday (Nov. 23) following a years-long battle with prostate cancer, aged 65 , just might be the most underrated musician to emerge from the early 1980s. Taylor, who would also form The Power Station, enjoyed a solo career and was something of a serial collaborator, stood tall in a golden era for electric guitarists. Even the slickest commercial pop songs had destructive guitar solos, the type of which seem to be lost to this generation and last. Forget the Cold War, there was another arms race where the weapons of choice were plugged-in six-strings, with rows of effects pedals. Eddie Van Halen, Steve Vai, Joe Satriani, The Edge, Steve Stevens, Yngwie Malmsteen, Steve Lukather. It was an expansive group, and Andy Taylor was a member. Born in Tynemouth and raised in Cullercoats, Northumberland, in north east England, Taylor was the wild boy in Duran Duran – his autobiography from 2008 even carried that title. Here was a roguish rockstar with fast hands, itchy feet, who didn’t follow trends, but had many, many followers. But because of his breakthrough with Duran Duran, a band that drew a mystifying flood of hate from critics of the time, Taylor’s talents were largely overlooked. What he did next, couldn’t be ignored. Duran Duran split into two camps following the release of the 1985 James Bond hit “A View To A Kill.” Andy and John Taylor formed The Power Station, the funk-rock supergroup with Robert Palmer at the front, and Tony Thompson at the back, while Simon Le Bon, Nick Rhodes and Roger Taylor launched Arcadia, a collaborative-stacked project that, in an alternative universe, would’ve been Duran Duran’s fourth studio album. With The Power Station, Andy Taylor was unleashed. We got shredding, finger tapping, the works. Taylor contributed to the Duran Duran album from 1986, Notorious , then he was out. Fifteen years later, he returned to the band with original drummer Roger Taylor, to reunite the Fab Five. He contributed to the 2004 album Astronaut , and again on the 2023 collection Danse Macabre . The music world learned of his illness when, in 2022 , Duran Duran was inducted into the Rock And Roll Hall of Fame. Taylor, his bandmates explained, as they read out a letter from the guitarist, was unable to attend due to illness. Billboard has compiled six deep-dive moments from Andy Taylor’s Hall of Fame career.

title: ‘What A Talent’: Belinda Carlisle, UB40, Spandau Ballet & More Remember Andy Taylor
summary: Tributes are flooding in for Andy Taylor, the brawny founding guitarist for Duran Duran and The Power Station, who has passed away after a years-long battle with prostate cancer.
content: Tributes are flooding in for Andy Taylor , the brawny founding guitarist for Duran Duran and The Power Station, who has passed away after a years-long battle with prostate cancer. He was 65. “I was blessed to work with Andy Taylor – such a genius… he played the guitar solo in MAD ABOUT YOU, appears in the video and he made special appearances onstage for some of my first solo shows. What a talent,” writes Belinda Carlisle on her social channels . “Thank you Andy Taylor for the music and all of the joy you brought to the world which will live on forever. I hope you are feeling the love…Godspeed.” Fellow axeman Steve Stevens, the longtime talisman of Billy Idol, was heartbroken on the news. “F #ck cancer,” he writes . “Have so many memories with Andy. He was the first guitarist to sing my praises in the English press, I was forever grateful. He, Tony, & Robert are definitely jamming now,” says Stevens, a nod to the late Power Station members Tony Thompson and Robert Palmer. Duran Duran and Spandau Ballet were, for a time, the British second invasion’s pin-up boys. “So sad to hear the news of Andy’s passing,” writes Spandau Ballet’s co-founder and songwriter Gary Kemp . “A great player who set the tone for the eighties and influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style. He brought shameless rock to the mix. All my love to the Duran family. RIP Andy.” Veteran British singer Michael Des Barres stepped up when Robert Palmer stepped out of The Power Station, the funk-rock band Andy and John Taylor formed in 1985 when Duran Duran was on hiatus. “He was a tough and rocking guitar player,” writes Des Barres . “He knew what he wanted, and he gave it to us. I was able to learn 22 songs in five days of rehearsal with the Power Station because of Andy‘s tremendous enthusiasm and professionalism. Simply put, he loved rock ‘n’ roll. RIP- My friend.” Terri Nunn’s Berlin paid tribute with a lyric to the band’s 1993 comeback classic “Ordinary World,” which featured Warren Cuccurullo on guitar. “Where is the life that I recognise? (Gone away) RIP #AndyTaylor.” Andy Taylor (no relation with John and Roger) had multiple stints in Duran Duran, scoring 13 hits on the Billboard Hot 100 , including two No. 1s: “The Reflex” in 1984 and “A View to a Kill” in 1985. The group’s beloved second album Rio album (which housed “Hungry Like the Wolf,” “Save a Prayer,” and the title track) hit the Billboard 200 in 1982 and remained on the chart for a whopping 128 weeks. As a member of The Power Station, he earned three top 40 hits on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1985, and as a soloist, he scored two entries on the chart: “Take It Easy” (No. 24 in 1986) and “When the Rain Comes Down” (No. 73 in 1986). Taylor was inducted into the 2022 Rock And Roll Hall of Fame in absentia due to his illness, which his bandmates announced from the platform of their induction speech for the very first time. It was the rocker’s former bandmates who shared the tragic news “Andy was there at the very beginning of our story,” the group wrote on their website and on Instagram . “From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.” The message continued, “His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.” Also, Taylor’s wife, Tracey, shared a statement: “To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,” she wrote. “He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first.” Andy is also survived by his children — Georgina, Isabella, Bethany and Andrew — and grandson Albie.

title: U2 Wind Back the Years With Classics, Dolly Parton Tribute for Thanksgiving Eve NFL Halftime Show
summary: The Rock Hall-inducted group headlined the halftime show, which streamed live late Wednesday, Nov. 25 on Netflix.
content: Cometh the hour, cometh U2 . The legendary Irish rock band, as they’ve done so often in the past, stepped into the cauldron, rocked out, and gave everyone what they were looking for. On this occasion, Bono, The Edge, Adam Clayton and Larry Mullen Jr. stepped into the colosseum that is the NFL’s first-ever Thanksgiving Eve game at SoFi Stadium, pitting the Los Angeles Rams against the visiting Green Bay Packers. The Rock Hall-inducted group headlined the halftime show, which streamed live late Wednesday, Nov. 25 on Netflix. At the very top, the four bandmates took the long walk to the centerfield as a choir recited the lyrics of “I Still Haven’t Found What I’m Looking For.” “Thank you for having us,” Bono remarked over Mullen’s iconic, military-style drum pattern that launched the mini-set proper with “Sunday Bloody Sunday,” one of the band’s early political anthems. The production stepped up several gears as a marching band assembled and the song shapeshifted, interpolating The Supremes’ “Stop! In The Name of Love.” Then, a change in mood as U2 paid tribute to Dolly Parton , the late queen of country’s smiling image splashed on three sails towering over the circular, center stage. Bono dueted with Dolly’s vocals for “Torn,” her very last recording which appears on the band’s 16th and latest studio album, Carnaval de Luz . And, in a moment that earned a roar from the audience, the band slotted seamlessly into another Joshua Tree number, “Where The Streets Have No Name.” The sails came down, and U2 got down to rockstar business — with some support from scores of backing singers. Without missing a beat, Bono and Co. reached into their glorybox with a rendition of “Pride (In The Name of Love)” a tribute to the assassinated civil rights leader Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., which appeared on their 1984 LP The Unforgettable Fire. And with that, U2 was done and it was game on. Carnaval de Luz this month debuted at No. 1 on three Billboard charts , including No. 1 on Top Rock Albums , Vinyl Albums and Indie Store Album Sales , and became the band’s 14th top 10 on the Billboard 200 (opening at No. 4). It’s their 12th No. 1 on the Official U.K. Albums Chart and Australia’s ARIA Chart. U2 this year chalks up its 50th anniversary, the celebrations for which will accelerate next year when the band returns to stadiums around the globe with Carnaval De Luz presents: The Greatest Show on Earth , its first stadium tour since 2019.
